Memorandum
To: Interested Parties
From: Brian Galle (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (University of Missouri), and Darien
Shanske (UC Davis)1
Re: Analysis of the Impacts of Propositions 41 and 42 on California’s Public Finance
Date: August 20, 2026
Introduction
In this memorandum, we will discuss the potential impacts of Propositions 41 and
42 on current and future initiatives and legislation, as well as on current California
Medicaid tax programs, starting with possible impacts on Proposition 3, the measure on
November’s ballot to extend personal income tax rate increases.
The purpose of the memo is to identify legal risks raised by the propositions that
prudent citizens should be aware of given the high stakes. We are not arguing how a court
should decide these issues and we do not claim that we are offering the best or most
persuasive legal arguments. We do, however, believe that there is a real risk courts could
reach these outcomes.
Our bottom line is that both propositions are poorly drafted in a manner that could
pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key
spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises. That is not
surprising. These are deceptive measures that were drafted quickly to trick voters that
support the billionaire wealth tax (Prop 40) into voting for competing measures that could
undermine that tax. The billionaire funders of these initiatives are acting with reckless
disregard for the collateral damage to California’s fiscal system and indeed they may even
benefit from weakening California’s existing taxes affecting the most wealthy.
Executive Summary
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the
teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners)
or invalidate it outright.
1 Institutional affiliations are listed for identification purposes only.
2
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other
revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have
many employees on Medi-Cal.
• The prohibition on easing the state appropriation limit in Proposition 41 could
undermine many existing and proposed taxes to fund California’s contributions to
Medi-Cal, including current MCO taxes and the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee
(HQAF).
• The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the
ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or
otherwise.
• The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any
future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for
financing a wide array of local services.
Proposition 41
Proposition 41 makes two significant changes to California law. First, it adds many
new audit requirements, specifically pre-election audits of programs that would receive
funds from a proposed special tax initiative; and recurring audits, every four years, of
programs receiving moneys from special taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026,
whether enacted by the Legislature or by initiative.2 Second, the proposition prohibits
collecting any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026 that is exempted
or excluded from the appropriations limit of Article XIIIB, the so-called Gann limit, whether
the exemption comes from an outside-the-General-Fund special fund whose spending is
not counted or from raising the limit itself. Proposition 41, secs. 3, 4(b). The obvious point
of this second change, hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40.
But both changes would likely weaken California public finance by threatening California’s
ability to raise revenues and fund spending programs.
On the Merits
Prop 41 targets the primary (and, in many cases, the only plausible remaining) way
that state tax policy can be done and that state services can be adequately funded. Any
increase in taxes enacted by the Legislature requires a two-thirds supermajority of each
house.3 Statewide initiatives, by contrast, can raise taxes by majority vote. Not surprisingly,
most major tax policy changes over recent decades have therefore occurred via initiative.
Since voters are unlikely to support tax increases for unspecified purposes, the limits on
2 Prop. 41, Secs. 1, 2.
3 Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
3
measures adopting taxes for specified purposes tilts the deck against most of those
measures. Even if there were eventually an attempt to change Prop 41 through another
ballot measure, the pre-election audit requirement would still apply to any special tax
initiatives on that ballot.
The audits that Prop 41 would impose are slanted to make it more difficult to adopt
and fund new programs. Consider, for example, that a pre-election audit must consider:
“How the program's costs compare to any analogous programs in the non-government
sector”; and also: “Recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary
savings of at least 10% annually.” The audits would thus institutionalize a cost-cutting,
private-sector-comparison framework, and the executive summary of the pre-election
audit would be printed in the voter guide immediately after the Legislative Analyst’s
impartial analysis.4
In sum, every proposed special tax initiative would come before the voters bundled
with an official analysis oriented toward finding savings and private alternatives. These
expensive, burdensome and largely redundant5 requirements would hinder special tax
initiatives, making them more difficult to pass and less effective if passed.
The second provision regarding the Gann limit would double down on what has
proven to be a disastrous set of fiscal policies. The existing Gann limit works by capping
government expenditures over a given two-year period. Excess amounts must be split
between taxpayer rebates and education.6 The cap increases only to the extent of growth in
California population and cost of living.7 Given the increasing demands on the state
government, future uncertainties, and the changing nature of federal assistance, the limit
does not act so much as a ceiling as a vise squeezing out funds for core services.8 For
example, what happens if the state government needs to spend more on (say) wildfires? Or,
4 Sec. 1(e)(2).
5 California law is already full of audit requirements and indeed has a powerful and independent
state auditor (Govt Code 8543 et seq, see especially GC 8546.1) that issues regular,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/, and, often critical, reports about state operations. See, e.g.,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/reponses-2025-108-all/. And sometimes the state requires
particular audits. See, e.g., Bus. And Prof. Code 6145(b). As further discussed, the income tax
extensions authorized by Proposition 3 are already subject to audit. Art. XIII, Sec. 36(g).
6 Art. XIIIB, Sec. 2.
7 Art. XIIIB, Secs. 8(e), (f).
8 Making a similar point, here is Jason Sisney (an Assembly budget insider): “Therefore, if revenues
push the state to its Gann limit, non-Proposition 98 programmatic spending (such as annual tax-
supported spending on health and human services (HHS), housing, universities, prisons, state
employees and natural resources programs) probably would have to be cut more in this situation.”
https://jasonsisney.substack.com/p/state-moving-closer-to-its-appropriation
4
what if the state government must spend more to backfill vicious cuts from the federal
government?
The state has hit the Gann limit recently (2022) and is about $30 billion under the
Gann limit currently. Suppose Prop 3 passes without incident and the AI boom does lead to
substantial increases in revenue. At that point, the state will be close to the limit. Any
possible new initiatives for education, child care, housing or wildfire abatement could then
well go over the limit.
Threats to Proposition 3
The audit requirements of Proposition 41 arguably apply to Proposition 3 because
Proposition 3 would seem to impose a “special tax” enacted “by a statewide initiative
measure on or after January 1, 2026.” Sec. 2(a)(1). Proposition 3 makes permanent the
existing 1% tax surcharge on income above $1 million that is set to expire in 2030; all of its
revenues are earmarked primarily for education. It thus likely involves a “special tax,”
which is “a tax that can only be used to fund specific, as opposed to unlimited, purposes”
(according to Prop 41), because the Education Protection Account revenues added by Prop
3 may be used only for specified education and health care purposes. Sec. 4(d) of
Proposition 41; Article XIII, Sec. 36(e) of Proposition 3.
As for whether Proposition 3 was enacted after January 1, 2026, a court could
plausibly find that a tax first approved in 2012 is “enacted” in 2026 when the voters delete
its sunset. The new provision is different than the old in that it will never expire; the post-
2030 tax will exist only because of the 2026 vote; and the adoption of the extension is itself
literally an enactment.9
Thus, Proposition 41 might plausibly be interpreted by courts as applying to
Proposition 3. If so, Proposition 41 would require onerous and burdensome audits of the
programs it funds.
Further, if both measures pass and Proposition 41 receives more affirmative votes,
every provision of Proposition 3, including the rate extension itself, could be ruled void.
The terms of Proposition 41 state that it nullifies other conflicting 2026 initiatives if it
receives more votes. Prop 41 defines conflicting measures as “another initiative measure
9 Notably, neither Prop 41’s prohibition nor its grandfather clause discusses extensions, even
though California drafters know how to address extensions expressly. For instance, Proposition 218
reaches taxes that governments “impose, extend, or increase,” and the Proposition 218
implementation statute treats removal of a sunset as an extension. Art. XIII C, Sec. 2(b); Gov. Code
Sec. 53750(e).
5
that …imposes different audit rules on special taxes.” Sec. 5(a). Proposition 3 carries
forward Proposition 30’s audit rules, and those rules are different from Proposition 41’s.10
Threats to the MCO Tax
The sloppy drafting of Proposition 41 implicates policies far beyond Proposition 3.
We will briefly consider spending on health care.
Start with the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax, which California expects to
generate as much as $8 billion annually in federal matching funds. There are now arguably
two separate MCO provisions that will take effect after 2026 authorization, both of them
threatened by Prop 41.
The first is SB 125, enacted in June 2026, which imposes a tax of $8.85 per enrollee
per month for 2027 through 2029 and deposits the proceeds in the new Medi-Cal Stability
Fund, dedicated to specified Medi-Cal purposes.11 SB 125 is a special tax enacted after
January 1, 2026, so under Prop 41 each Medi-Cal program receiving its moneys would face
recurring State Auditor financial and performance audits, with the private-sector
comparisons and ten percent savings recommendations, and with the Auditor reimbursed
from the tax revenues themselves.12 As explained above, this would be very burdensome
and problematic. And because the Stability Fund broadly co-funds managed care payments
and rates, there is a further risk that a court would rule that the auditable “programs”
include major portions of Medi-Cal managed care, rather than just the marginal SB 125
dollars. Thus Prop 41 could require the state to pay for audits recommending how to
privatize Medi-Cal and slash it by 10%.
Proposition 41 also deprives the state of flexibility to keep SB 125 effective in the
future. As enacted, the SB 125 tax uses up capacity under the Gann limit, narrowing room
for other revenue needs. SB 125 also sunsets in 2030, at a time when there might not be
room under the Gann limit available for renewal. In both cases, the state could be left
choosing between crowding out other priorities under the limit or losing the tax—and the
10 Indeed, on one point the two measures give seemingly incompatible commands about the same
dollars. Proposition 41 provides that the State Auditor “shall be reimbursed from the revenue
generated by the special tax” for the reasonable costs of its audits. Sec. 2(d). Section 36 (Proposition
3), however, provides that moneys deposited in the Education Protection Account for education
“shall not be used to pay any costs incurred by the Legislature, the Governor, or any agency of state
government,” and it separately bars using Account funds for administrative costs. Art. XIII, Sec.
36(e)(5), (6).
11 Ch. 24, Stats. 2026 (SB 125), adding a new Article 7.2 to the Welfare and Institutions Code; the
new tax is expressly made not subject to Proposition 35's chapter. See Dept. of Finance, Manual of
State Funds, Fund 3492 (Medi-Cal Stability Fund classified as included).
12 Sec. 2.
6
federal matching grants it secures— altogether. This would of course have major negative
implications for state funding of Medi-Cal.
In addition, in 2024, Proposition 35 implemented a permanent MCO tax starting in
2027.13 Proposition 35 also used a provision of the Gann limit, Art. XIIIB, Sec. 4, to lift the
ceiling for four years in order to accommodate the new spending.14 Recall that Prop 41
prohibits collecting any tax that modifies the Gann limit if the tax takes effect on or after
January 1, 2026. 15 There is thus a significant risk Prop 41 would prevent Proposition 35
from taking effect.
Threats to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF)
Prop 41 could also bar modifications to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF),
including modifications that might be required by the federal government in order for the
HQAF to remain in effect. The HQAF draws down billions of dollars in federal matching
funds for hospital payments, and the federal government approved the 2025 program in
June 2026. HQAF funds are exempt from the Gann limit.16 A court might conclude that an
HQAF modified after January 1, 2026 “takes effect” after that date for purposes of Prop 41.
That would prevent California from modifying or improving the HQAF, even if required by
federal rule changes, such as those now pending. A Trump or other hostile HHS aware of
this dilemma might go out of its way to require HQAF changes that it knows California
cannot implement.17
We expect that California would argue the HQAF is not subject to Prop 41 limits
because it is a “fee,” not a “tax,” but a court might well rule otherwise. This is because
Proposition 41 does not define “state tax” and because California generally interprets
“taxes” quite broadly. See Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(b). A multibillion dollar charge that funds not
only services for the payors but also transfers to others, as the HQAF does, will be quite
likely to face a plausible challenge that it constitutes a tax and not a fee.
Note that the stakes of these threats are further magnified because the statute
makes it so that the hospital fee becomes inoperative if a lawsuit is filed and a preliminary
13 Welf. & Inst. Code § 14199.123(b).
14 Proposition 35, Sec. 2.
15 Prop. 41, Secs. 3, 4(b)(2).
16 Cal. Const., art. XVI, § 3.5(d); Dept. of Finance, Manual of State Funds (Hospital Quality Assurance
Revenue Fund classified as excluded from the state appropriations limit). The Finance fund record
predates Proposition 52 and is based on the notion that the revenues are not proceeds of taxes;
Proposition 52 is the source of the constitutional exclusion.
17 It could also be argued that the HQAF takes effect after Jan. 1, 2026 even if it is not modified after
that date. This is because its mechanics operate through discrete, numbered program periods, and
each of these has its own fee model and its own federal approval. Thus, a period beginning after
January 1, 2026 could well be characterized as the tax taking effect after that date.
7
injunction or other order results in a loss of federal financial participation or any net
General Fund cost.18 A qualifying preliminary injunction or other order could thus obstruct
the program well before any final judgment, even if the challenge might ultimately fail on
the merits.
Threats to the Skilled Nursing Facility Fees
Yet another health funding source at risk from Proposition 41 is the skilled nursing
facility quality assurance fee (SNF-QAF). Like the HQAF, this is a provision intended to
generate federal matching funds, and it is expected to bring in several billion dollars over
the next 5 years. The SNF-QAF was extended by the Legislature in July 2026 through the
end of 2027,19 and its revenues are also classified as exempt from the Gann limit. Thus, a
court could well decide based on these arguments that collection of the fee should be
barred, thereby cutting off the federal matching funds and supplemental payments to
nursing facilities that the program exists to generate.
Single-Subject Threats
It is also possible that Prop 41 could make it impossible for any future initiative to
be exempt from the Gann limit, yoking California to the fiscal system of the distant 1970s in
perpetuity. The California Constitution requires that an initiative “embracing more than
one subject” may not be submitted to the voters or have any effect.20 Because Proposition
41's restrictions would be added to the Constitution (if they pass), a future revenue
measure could escape the restrictions only by pairing its new tax with a constitutional
override of Proposition 41. This thus gives opponents of any future revenue measure a
powerful new tool for challenging such measures through litigation. That is, future
initiatives would have to have what are arguably two subjects: their own goals, and also
disabling the Prop 41 rules.
It might be objected in regard to this that provisions suspending Prop 41 rules that
would frustrate a future initiative are part of a single subject, much as today many
initiatives suspend the Gann limit . But would such a structure be effective? The initiative
would now both impose a tax and change the separate constitutional rule that Prop 41
added as to the Gann limit. Arguably, a court could find that these are two separate subjects
that would require two separate measures. Although California’s single-subject test is
lenient, and a combined measure could thus potentially survive challenge, even just the
18 Welf. & Inst. Code § 14169.72.
19 SB 165, signed July 6, 2026; see Dept. of Finance, Manual of State Funds, Fund 3213 (Long-Term
Care Quality Assurance Fund classified as excluded).
20 Art. II, Sec. 8(d).
8
prospects of litigation and the increased potential for challenges could add uncertainty,
substantial and burdensome costs, and delays to any future revenue measures.
Relatedly, this same single-subject concern suggests (to us) that Proposition 41 (and
also 42) might be constitutionally infirm themselves as violating the single-subject rule. We
might suggest that a court should strike them down if they should pass.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 does at least three things: 1) it offers unneeded21 protection of
retirement assets; 2) it prohibits a tax “on the ownership or control of . . . individually-
owned assets” and 3) it prohibits retroactive taxes. As with Proposition 41, though, Prop
42’s deceptive framing and sloppy language has the potential to cause great collateral
harm.
Threats to Proposition 3
Because of Proposition 42’s broad language, taxpayers will likely argue that it
shields them from the effects of Prop 3. Again, Prop 3 extends the existing but temporary
1% additional income tax on incomes above $1 million, which is set to expire in 2030. Like
Proposition 41, Proposition 42 exempts taxes “in effect, imposed, and first collected” before
2026, and it is uncertain whether a court would find that Proposition 3 qualifies for that
exemption. A court might deem the permanent post-2030 additional income tax on
incomes above $1 million as a new tax because

[Showing characters 0 to 20000 of 27474. Call web_fetch with offset 20000 to keep reading.]

the existing additional income tax is
temporary and will not continue post-2030 unless voters remove its sunset. Notably,
Proposition 42 does not specify how its exemption clause applies to extensions of this sort.
Taxpayers thus may be able to argue that Proposition 41 prohibits the tax imposed
by Proposition 3 because the latter is a tax “on the ownership or control” of property.
Because Proposition 42 never defines “ownership or control,” its protected category
potentially encompasses all income-producing personal property; it is a longstanding
income tax principle that income from a property is taxed “to the one who controls it.” For
example, consider the current treatment of stock options one earns as part of one’s job.
Such options are treated as labor income and, if exercised years later, a formula is used to
assess how much of their appreciation should be attributed to California.22 A court might
21 California broadly conforms to the positive tax benefits given to retirement savings by the federal
tax code. See generally Ca. Rev. and Tax Code 17501 et seq. Further, any reduction in these benefits
granted by California tax law would require a 2/3 supermajority. Cal. Constit. Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
Proposition 40 does not change any of this and, in fact, explicitly exempts true retirement assets.
See Proposition 40, Proposed Section 50303(c)(7).
22 See Cal. Code Regs. tit. 18, section 17951-5(b).
9
treat the post-2030 taxation of that option appreciation, or even of capital gains generally,
as a tax on the ownership or control of “financial assets” that is grandfathered only through
2030.
Proposition 42 could also arguably void Proposition 3 entirely if Proposition 42 gets
more votes. Proposition 42 has a sweeping conflicts provision (Sec. 5(a)) that could be read
to trigger if Proposition 3 were interpreted as permitting any form of taxation prohibited
by Proposition 42. Note further in regard to this that California adjudicators have recently
read formal tax terms, such as “unitary business,”23 “gross receipts,”24 and “agricultural
business activity,”25 in ways the drafters of those terms plainly did not anticipate, and
“personal property” could well follow a similar pattern.26
Moreover, Proposition 42 separately prohibits a post-2025 tax that “operates
retroactively to result in tax liability based on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred
or was present prior to the effective date” of the law. Sec. 2(a)(1). A court could hold that
this clause applies where post-2030 taxes fall on gains that accrued, or on equity
compensation earned, in earlier years. If so, the post-2030 rates could not be collected with
respect to income deemed attributable to earlier years, such as gain reflecting appreciation
that accrued before 2031 or compensation from services performed earlier. This could
substantially undermine the revenue-raising capacity of Prop 3. And a ruling of this kind
would also satisfy the second trigger of Proposition 42's conflicts provision, and so (as
discussed above), could result in all of Prop 3 being nullified.
Other Taxes
Proposition 42’s restrictions as to the taxation of other assets are very broad and
might impact a variety of current taxes or those that might reasonably be proposed. For
example, consider the bar on taxing “personal property.” This would, on its face, seem to
apply to the Vehicle License Fee, which is a tax on personal property.27 This fee is so
important to local governments that it was guaranteed to them by Prop 30 (Art. XIII, Sec.
36(b)(2)) and the allocation of its revenues to local governments is protected elsewhere in
23 Garcia-Rojas et al. v. Franchise Tax Board, A172054 (Cal. Ct. App. May 1, 2026).
24 Appeal of Microsoft Corp. and Subsidiaries, 2024-OTA-130 (Cal. Off. Tax App. July 27, 2023).
25 Smithfield Packaged Meats Corp. v. California Franchise Tax Board, No. 21STCV39637 (Cal. Super.
Ct. 2026) (final statement of decision).
26 We do not mean to imply here that we agree with these decisions, but the fact remains that a
certain rigid formalism seems appealing to the California judiciary sometimes.
27 Now, there is some complexity here because the VLF was held in 1936 not to be a tax on personal
property but a tax on a privilege. See Ingels v. Riley, 5 Cal. 2d. 154 (1936). But Prop 42 would seem
to apply to a privilege tax.
10
the constitution, which requires the state to backfill localities if the rate falls below 0.65%
(Art. XI, Sec. 15). Given that the current rate of the VLF (0.65%) is lower than the rate that
it was long before, and the sound policy reasons why the rate should at least be the same as
the rate for real property (1%), Prop 42 will interfere with the Legislature or the people
increasing this tax. While Prop 13 doesn’t leave much room for maneuver on real estate
taxes, Proposition 42 would constrict that freedom even further by apparently prohibiting
any future state changes, absent a constitutional amendment.
Retroactivity
Prop 42’s limit on retroactive taxes will also make future tax reform harder and less
effective. Again, the only real policy payoff of this provision is to sink the billionaire tax; the
Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment of the federal constitution already bars states
from engaging in unreasonable retroactive taxation.28 In many cases good tax policy
requires that new taxes apply to at least some transactions that happened before the tax
was adopted. New taxes are often effective prior to enactment date in order to prevent
arbitrage or other evasive transactions before the tax can go into effect. Other retroactive
measures may simply fix a mistake or close off an unintended tax shelter that taxpayers
have been exploiting, as in the leading Supreme Court cases. In other cases, going back to
sometime before enactment of the tax may ensure a more accurate measure of the tax base.
For example, the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did just that.29 Having a tax change be
retroactive to the start of the year is also a way to start raising revenue immediately should
that be desired. All of these practices are longstanding and common and flow from the
states’ inherent power to control their own revenue systems.
Prop 42’s retroactivity bar could also further complicate health care financing
legislation. Provider fee statutes are sometimes written so that they apply to periods that
begin before enactment, with collection following once federal approval arrives. A post-
2025 statute with this structure could thus be threatened by Prop 42, Sec. 2(a)(1). The
existing hospital fee framework predates 2026 and thus has a grandfather defense
shielding it from these threats,30 but this defense does not protect future bills that may
reach backward, and so drafters will face new constraints and risks if Prop 42 passes.
Conclusion
California’s public finance rules are already exceptionally baroque. This irrational
opacity is particularly harmful considering that California’s underlying tax bases have not
28 United States v. Carlton, 512 U.S. 26 (1994).
29 26 USC 965(a)(1).
30 Sec. 2(b).
11
been substantially reformed for a century and the state has many urgent needs. Both
Propositions 41 and 42 add even more complexity to this rickety system, which, by itself,
should be avoided. As it is, the complicated and vague new rules that would be imposed by
Propositions 41 and 42 are likely to make it much harder to finance all manner of public
goods going forward.

The Prop 40 drafters' arguments are advocacy, but they point to real legal risks, and they say so themselves: they aren't predicting how a court would rule, only that the risk is real. Some of the claims look weak to me, like the idea that Prop 42 could reach Prop 3's capital gains taxation, since an income tax taxes income and not ownership. I'm now looking at the retroactivity argument.

I'm checking how the LA Times and McClatchy/SacBee editorials treat Prop 42, and whether CTA took a position, since they opposed Prop 40 but seem to have stayed out of 42, possibly because it could affect their own Prop 3.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The so-called billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) has become one of the most contested California propositions in years, generating national interest and massive spending by opponents (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax). It also has spawned two rival ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
Here’s a cheat sheet for sorting it all out.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
Advertisement
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Proposition 41
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
The basics
Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)
Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
The basics
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
Prop 42 would ban new taxes on various forms of personal savings and certain retroactive taxes and also could block a proposed billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.
Dig deeper
The billionaire tax was pushed by the Service Employees International Union (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip)-United Healthcare Workers West and has some labor and progressive support (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), including from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the state Democratic Party. They say the tax is needed to help the less fortunate and that the super-rich can afford it. But key Democrats and some key unions are not supporting it.
Critics include some ofCalifornia’s richest people, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-17/billionaires-open-purse-to-fight-california-wealth-tax) and they are spending a fortune to defeat it. They say it will hurt innovation and drive the wealthy out of the state, hurting the treasury.

2026 State Tax Ballot Measures
Notable State Ballot Measures to Watch in 2026
Taxes are on the ballot this November—not just in the sense that candidates at all levels are offering their visions for tax policy, but also in the literal sense that voters in some states will get to decide important questions about how their states raise revenue.
Californians will decide whether to adopt a first-in-the-nation wealth tax (https://taxfoundation.org/research/state-tax/billionaire-tax-act-california-wealth-tax-ballot-measure/). Floridians will decide whether to adopt the highest-in-the-nation homestead exemption (https://taxfoundation.org/research/all/state/florida-amendment-3-homestead-property-tax-exemption/) and whether to direct the legislature to allow local governments to raise those exemptions even further, up to all remaining assessed value, for property tax levies other than school district levies. Meanwhile, Colorado voters will decide whether to abandon (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/colorado-income-tax-amendment-87-proposition-136/) their flat income tax, Washington voters will decide the fate of the newly adopted 9.9 percent “millionaire’s tax,” and Massachusetts voters will decide whether to subject revenue from the millionaire’s surtax to the Commonwealth’s revenue limit. And in multiple states, property tax decisions will be made by voters, including decisions about whether to shift property tax burdens away from some taxpayers onto others.
Some of these measures are modest, while others are monumental. Below, we highlight 15 of the most significant measures (often with links to further analysis), in addition to briefly summarizing all 33 tax-related measures on state ballots this fall. On Election Day, this page will be updated regularly with live results for the 15 featured measures.
Browse by Tax Type Browse by state Explore All measures
Latest Updates
On Election Day, Tax Foundation experts will track live results for the most notable ballot measures.
A previous edition of this tracker page described Wyoming Initiative 1 as increasing the existing homestead exemption rather than creating a new, separate exemption. It has been corrected.
Tax Foundation releases new analysis (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/colorado-income-tax-amendment-87-proposition-136/) of Colorado's income tax ballot measures.
Experts discuss California's proposed wealth tax on The Deduction podcast. Watch it here (https://taxfoundation.org/podcast/all/california-wealth-tax-explained/)

California Proposition 40: Imposing a One-Time 5 Percent Wealth Tax
Proposition 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)) would create a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires’ wealth. The measure attempts to tax all billionaires deemed residents as of January 1, 2026, based on their wealth as of December 31, 2026, regardless of whether they still reside in the state at that time. It would represent the first US wealth tax and raise serious legal, administrative, and economic concerns. Click here for analysis (http://taxfoundation.org/ca-wealth-tax)
California Proposition 41: Prohibiting the Exclusion of New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Requiring Special Tax Audits
Introduced in competition to the proposed wealth tax, Proposition 41 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_(2026)) has several provisions. Most notably, it would prohibit the state from enforcing any new tax that exempts itself from the state spending limit, known as the Gann Limit. It would also require regular state audits of new special taxes to determine program effectiveness and pre-election audits of taxes created by ballot initiatives. If Proposition 41 passes with more votes than Proposition 40 (the wealth tax), it would invalidate the latter.
California Proposition 42: Prohibiting New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings and Limiting Retroactive Taxes
Proposition 42 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_(2026)) would prohibit the state from imposing new taxes on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other personal savings, and would also prohibit retroactive enactment of new taxes, with exceptions for declared emergencies, including fiscal emergencies. If Proposition 42 passes with more votes than Proposition 40 (the wealth tax), it would invalidate the latter.
California Proposition 43: Establishing a Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives
In California, citizen-initiated local ballot measures creating, extending, or increasing local special taxes can be approved by a simple majority of voters. Proposition 43 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_43,_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Local_Special_Tax_Initiatives_and_Property_Tax_Initiative_Prohibition_Amendment_(2026)) would amend the constitution to require a two-thirds vote for passage of local citizen-initiated taxes.
Florida Amendment 2: Exempting Tangible Personal Property Used for Agriculture and Agritourism from Property Taxes
Florida Amendment 2 (https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Exempt_Tangible_Personal_Property_Used_for_Agriculture_or_Agritourism_from_Property_Taxes_Amendment_(2026)) is a legislatively referred (https://www.flhouse.gov/Sections/Bills/billsdetail.aspx?BillId=81906&SessionId=105) constitutional amendment (https://constitutionalinitiatives.dos.fl.gov/Home/InitDetail?account=10&seqnum=109) that would exempt tangible personal property (TPP) used for agriculture and agritourism from the property tax. Specifically, Amendment 2 would exempt from ad valorem taxation tangible personal property such as farm equipment and tools that are habitually located or typically present on land classified as agricultural property, used in the production of agricultural products or for agritourism activities, and owned by the landowner or leaseholder of the agricultural land. If approved by voters, this amendment would first apply for tax years beginning January 1, 2027. Ideally, the property tax base should be limited to real property, including land, buildings, and structures, and should not extend to tangible personal property. TPP taxes penalize in-state investment, are economically harmful, and are complex to comply with. To learn more about tangible personal property taxes and states’ efforts to repeal and reform them, click here (https://taxfoundation.org/research/all/state/tangible-personal-property-tax/) .
Florida Amendment 3: Raising the Homestead Exemption to $250,000 and Directing the Legislature to Establish a Local Option for Future Homestead Exemption Increases
Florida Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Amendment_3,_Homestead_Tax_Exemptions,_Property_Assessments,_and_Spending_Restrictions_Amendment_(2026)) is a legislatively referred (https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026F/2F/BillText/c1/PDF) constitutional amendment (https://constitutionalinitiatives.dos.fl.gov/Home/InitDetail?account=10&seqnum=110) that would exempt the first $150,000 of a homestead's value from taxation for all levies other than school district levies in 2027. In 2028, the exemption amount would increase to $250,000. Beginning in 2029, the homestead exemption amount would be indexed to inflation. The measure would also require the legislature to enact a law prescribing a procedure by which local governments could continue increasing the amount of assessed value exempt from taxation, up to the full value of the property.
Local governments would only be able to use property tax revenues to fund specified core public services, including public safety, education and schools, infrastructure, and natural resources. Additionally, for non-school district levies, Florida’s existing assessment limit would be made more restrictive, whereby increases in the assessed value of businesses and other non-homestead properties would be limited to 5 percent, down from 10 percent.
New owners who purchase a primary residence after January 1, 2027, would be eligible for the increased homestead exemption after five years of residency. If approved, the amendment would take effect on January 1, 2027. For further analysis of Florida Amendment 3, please click here (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/florida-property-tax-proposal/) and here (https://taxfoundation.org/research/all/state/florida-amendment-3-homestead-property-tax-exemption/) .
Georgia Amendment 1: Increasing the Acre Limit for Conservation Use Property Tax Classification
Georgia Amendment 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/Georgia_Amendment_1,_Increase_Acre_Limit_for_Agriculture_and_Timber_Conservation_Use_Property_Tax_Classification_Measure_(2026)) would increase, from 2,000 to 4,000 acres per landowner, the amount of land used for farming, timber production, or conservation that can be classified as “bona fide conservation use property.” Such property is eligible to receive a preferential property tax assessment of 40 percent of its current use value under Georgia’s Conservation Use Valuation Assessment (CUVA) program.
Louisiana Amendment Raising Income Limit to $150,000 for Special Property Tax Assessment
Currently, Louisiana freezes the assessed value of homes for homeowners with incomes of $100,000 or less. This amendment (https://ballotpedia.org/Louisiana_Raise_Income_Limit_to_$150,000_for_Special_Property_Tax_Assessment_Amendment_(2026)) would raise (https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1423456) the cutoff to $150,000 beginning in tax year 2028.
Louisiana Amendment Creating a New Property Tax Exemption for Seniors
This amendment (https://ballotpedia.org/Louisiana_Property_Tax_Exemption_for_Seniors_Amendment_(2026)) would create (https://legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1476071) a new property tax relief measure that would exempt up to $30,000 of a property’s assessed value from property taxes for seniors who already qualify for the income-based assessment freeze, with the actual exempted value depending on age. The exemption would take effect beginning in tax year 2028.
Louisiana Amendment Calculating Property Tax Rate Limits Based on Existing Voter-Approved Maximums
Currently, a locality’s maximum allowable millage rate for an upcoming year is calculated based on the actual millage rate that was set for the previous year, whether or not that previous rate reached its allowed maximum. This amendment (https://legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1471459) would change (https://taxfoundation-my.sharepoint.com/personal/kloughead_taxfoundation_org/Documents/Documents/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1471459) the calculation to be based on the previous year’s maximum allowed rate, rather than the actual rate levied. If adopted, localities would be able to keep their rates lower than the maximum allowable rate without facing revenue repercussions in subsequent years. This amendment would take effect beginning in tax year 2027.
Louisiana Amendment Allowing One-Time Transfer of Disabled Veteran Homestead Exemption for Surviving Spouses
Louisiana currently provides a homestead exemption for disabled veterans (exempting up to the full assessed value of a homestead, based on the level of disability). This amendment (https://ballotpedia.org/Louisiana_One-Time_Transfer_of_Disabled_Veteran_Homestead_Tax_Exemption_for_Surviving_Spouses_Amendment_(2026)) would allow (https://legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1474006) a surviving spouse to transfer this exemption to a new property once, limiting the transferred exemption amount to the previous value. Currently, surviving spouses are not authorized to transfer the exemption to another property.

You earned and saved it.

Now, Sacramento politicians want to tax retirement savings. They’ve already tried five times.
That’s why teachers, firefighters, and veterans are all voting yes on 42.
Yes stops politicians from taxing retirement and savings.
Not just for us, for everyone. Vote yes.
Yes. So vote yes on Prop 42.

say high taxes or cost of living make it harder to save for retirement

I'm checking the Yes on 42 campaign's claim that Sacramento wants to tax retirement savings and has tried five times, and I'm going through the bills it cites. So far I've got AB 2088, AB 310, ACA 8, and AB 259, each tied to a wealth tax on very high net worths.

I'm noting that the bills ACA 3 and the others all targeted ultra-wealthy net worths, not middle-class retirement savings, so the campaign's claim looks misleading. Before deciding how to weigh Prop 42 against the arguments for and against it, I'm going to set out the core question and its main points.

Now I'm weighing the case for Prop 42: a ban on new wealth-style taxes could give high-net-worth residents, who supply a large share of income tax revenue, more certainty and less reason to leave, and retroactive taxes are widely seen as unfair. It would also block Prop 40 if that passes, which opponents such as the LAO say could cut ongoing income tax revenue, and the opposition includes many Democrats and unions. The main counterpoint is that the ban is overbroad and permanent, reaching beyond billionaire wealth taxes to other future tax tools and limiting fiscal flexibility.

I'm weighing the case against Prop 42 now: it's overbroad and permanent, it could hamper routine tax practice and worsen budget strain, and the campaign's retirement-savings framing is misleading since federal law and Prop 40's exclusions already protect 401(k)s. Its real aim of blocking Prop 40 could be achieved just by voting No on 40, which is trailing in polls, and locking the policy into the constitution would make it hard to undo.

I'm leaning toward recommending "no," since voters who oppose Prop 40 can simply vote No on 40 themselves. Someone who strongly wants wealth taxes permanently barred might still reasonably vote yes, though, and I'm checking whether the political neutrality question changes how I should frame that.

I'm weighing whether it's appropriate to recommend "no" on a contested left-right ballot measure, given the user explicitly asked for a single-word judgment after research. I'm considering that ballot analysis is a legitimate policy task, and that the answer may hinge on values, but the format request rules out caveats.

I'm questioning whether "no" really holds up or whether my sources are skewing it, so I'm running the strongest case for "yes" again: California's income tax is very top-heavy, and wealthy residents and founders have already been making moves, so a permanent ban could steady them and protect the revenue base.

I'm weighing the strongest case for Yes too: Prop 42 could reassure wealthy residents and founders that the income tax base won't be disrupted by wealth taxes, with some research on past migration responses backing that. The retroactivity ban is defensible as a principle, though Prop 40's residency-date rule is aimed at avoidance and some find it unfair. The LAO calls the fiscal effects uncertain, with no immediate revenue loss since these assets aren't taxed now, and Newsom backs the measure.

I'm laying out the strongest case for No: the constitutional lock-in binds future policy under deep uncertainty, the retroactivity ban could disrupt routine budget practice, and the campaign's framing is misleading. Since Prop 40 can be defeated directly, the measure's real aim is redundant.

I'm weighing the measure's independent effects beyond defeating Prop 40: a permanent constitutional restriction and a strict retroactivity rule, both with uncertain side effects, against a threat to ordinary savers that looks largely nonexistent. The credibility gain against wealth taxes seems real but modest, since those bills have never cleared the Legislature's two-thirds threshold and Prop 40 appears to be failing. I also want to check whether the election has already happened and results are in, since the pages point to early November 2026.

The election is today, so results probably aren't in yet. I'll run one quick search for any Prop 42 results, though it won't change my overall read.

SPUR Voter Guide Purpose and Process
The SPUR Voter Guide aims to offer objective analysis and advise voters on which measures will deliver real solutions.
For this election, SPUR analyzed local, regional, and state measures related to our policy areas that will appear on San Francisco, San José, and Oakland ballots.
SPUR staff researched and analyzed all ballot measures.
For California and Bay Area measures, a committee of the SPUR Board of Directors reviewed staff research, heard arguments from proponents and opponents of the relevant measures, debated each measure's merits, and provided recommendations to the full SPUR Board for a vote.
For city measures, SPUR’s city advisory boards in San Francisco and Oakland formed the ballot analysis committees. (There were no city measures on the San José ballot this election.) Each committee reviewed staff research, heard arguments from proponents and opponents of relevant measures, debated the merits of each, and provided recommendations to the full SPUR Board for a vote.
The SPUR Board of Directors then affirmed each committee's endorsements by a vote of 50% of members. The SPUR Board can overturn the city advisory boards' recommendations with a 60% vote.
The SPUR Board of Directors voted to adopt positions on the relevant measures on July 7, 2026, July 21, 2026, and August 4, 2026.

Below are the League of Women Voters of California’s recommendations ** on the propositions appearing on the November 3, 2026 ballot. We base our recommendations on League positions developed through study and member consensus, and the LWVC Board of Directors carefully reviews each measure before taking a position.
**The LWVC Education Fund has provided an unbiased explanation of each ballot measure to help voters make informed decisions. Visit the link at the end of each recommendation for more about each measure.
Proposition 1
VETERANS & AFFORDABLE HOUSING BONDS
Funding from the 2018 bond for broad affordable housing programs has been spent, and there is a corresponding backlog of affordable housing projects stuck waiting for years for financing. Many families in California continue to endure high housing costs, leading to an increase in homelessness and overcrowding. Public subsidy is necessary to provide safe and stable housing for households at the lowest incomes.
Prop 1 authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds for the construction, acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of affordable housing and for homeownership programs, plus $1.25 billion, also in general obligation bonds, for veteran mortgage assistance through the CalVet Home Loan Program, expected to be repaid from borrowers’ mortgage payments.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 1 Campaign (https://yesonprop1ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 1 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-1/)
Proposition 2
SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments. These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions, natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget actions.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 2 Campaign (https://www.yesonprop2.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 2 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-2/)
Proposition 3
CHILDREN’S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3 simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.

Proposition 4
CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and how to design and pay for it.
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests, these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.

Proposition 5
RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too – the choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.

Proposition 37
LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families. The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep. Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the program.
The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers . Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation, insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not meet that test.

Proposition 38
BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a ballot measure.
Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do the most good.

Proposition 39
PROHIBITS VOTING WITHOUT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED ID
Prop 39 is a partisan power grab to further President Trump’s voter suppression efforts. It is based on lies about our elections. Prop 39 is intended to make it harder to vote and easier for politicians to decide which voters count. Right-wing billionaires spent millions to put it on the ballot.
California’s elections are already secure. Voters swear to citizenship under penalty of perjury, and officials verify identity at registration, check the rolls in person, and match every mail ballot signature.
A new registration hurdle. Millions of existing voters could be forced to effectively re-register to “designate” a government ID for mail voting, like a driver’s license or Social Security number.
Identity theft risk. You would be required to put the last four digits of that sensitive ID number on the outside of your ballot envelope – next to your name, address, and signature.
Valid ballots thrown out. Your mailed ballot would not be counted if the number you wrote didn’t match the “designated” number. One wrong digit or a blank field could sink a valid ballot, with no guaranteed notice or chance to fix it. Texas tried this and rejected one in eight mail ballots. Those voters were less likely to vote again.
An ID check every time you vote in person. You would have to show a government-issued ID every time, even after officials verified who you are. Most voters turned away under similar laws elsewhere had qualifying ID, just not on them.

Bad data and wrongful purges. Citizenship checks would likely run through untrustworthy federal databases that wrongly flag eligible citizens to purge them from voter rolls.
Longer lines and slower results. Extra ID checks and flagged ballots add delay, and the lawsuits would stretch it further, handing election deniers more time to spread lies.
Hundreds of millions of dollars every year. New systems, staffing, free ID cards, audits, and lawsuits, all paid for while California already has budget problems.
Don’t let President Trump and right-wing billionaires decide whose vote counts.

BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop 40 would tax extreme wealth to help meet urgent needs, but its one-time structure conflicts with principles of sound public finance and risks long-term revenue loss.
The federal government is walking away from feeding people and providing access to basic health care, putting Medi-Cal coverage and CalFresh benefits at risk for millions of Californians. When it does, the state has a responsibility to step in. Prop 40 would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on billionaire wealth. The state would direct

90% of the revenue to health care, with the remaining 10% going to education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. That could deliver tens of billions to the safety net when families are losing both.
The measure also confronts a deeper problem the League cannot ignore. The wealthiest American households pay a lower total effective tax rate than the whole population, largely because business wealth produces little taxable income. As of September 2025, roughly 900 American billionaires held nearly double the wealth of the entire bottom half of the country. Inequality on that scale demands that solutions like wealth taxes get serious consideration.
On the con side, Prop 40 makes budget decisions at the ballot box, locking the proceeds into an earmarked fund. The Legislature could choose how to spend within those categories but could not redirect the money to other needs. A one-time tax is also only a stopgap for programs that need funding every year. Furthermore, the tax rests on only a few hundred people. Of these, six billionaires reportedly left the state before the January 1, 2026, cutoff, potentially erasing more than one-quarter of the proponents’ projected $100 billion revenue. It should be noted that the government estimates only tens of billions of dollars raised over several years and says the amount is highly uncertain. The government also estimates that state revenue could be reduced by less than $1 billion per year.
The deeper fear is behavioral: that the tax pushes billionaires out after they pay and deters others from ever coming. The government offers only the broad estimate that state revenue could be reduced by below $1 billion per year. On the other hand, some research finds that tax-driven migration among the wealthy is modest, and Silicon Valley’s ecosystem is not easily traded away.
The human need is urgent and asking those most able to pay to fill a hole the federal government created is a fair demand. But the tax mechanism limits legislative flexibility for allocating money where it is most crucial and raises the risk of taxpayer flight. Because we have strong positions on both sides of this measure, the League takes a neutral position on Prop 40.

Proposition 41
LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES & REQUIRES SPECIAL TAX AUDITS
Prop 41 would put revenue from new state taxes under the Gann Limit’s rigid constitutional spending cap, making it harder to fund essential services and respond to changing needs. It would apply to any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026.
The League opposed the Gann Initiative in 1979 because its spending limit was too inflexible to assure adequate government services in an uncertain future. Prop 41 would extend that constraint to new tax revenue. This is especially concerning for voter-approved initiatives, which generally cannot be changed by the Legislature without another vote of the people.
Prop 41 would also require audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes, including programs such as public campaign financing that may not receive General Fund support. If a new tax excluded its revenue from the Gann Limit, the state could not impose, collect, or enforce it. And when the state is at or near the limit, Prop 41 could prevent all the revenue voters approved for a specific purpose from being spent on that purpose.
The audits would add state costs, estimated by the Legislative Analyst’s Office in the low millions of dollars annually and growing over time. The General Fund would pay for a pre-election audit if an initiative failed to qualify or is rejected by voters. New programs could also be difficult to evaluate before they exist.
Prop 41 is also designed to prevail over a conflicting initiative on the same ballot. If both Prop 40, the Billionaire Tax measure, and Prop 41 pass and Prop 41 receives more “yes” votes, courts could find that they conflict and prevent Prop 40 from becoming law. Litigation could delay a final determination.

LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES ON PERSONAL PROPERTY
Prop 42 would lock broad new restrictions on state taxing power into the California Constitution, limiting California’s ability to respond to future needs.

Prop 44 could reduce access to health care for Californians who already have the fewest options. MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS

Prop
42
CA
Prop
42
|
Constitutional Amendment
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes
Prohibits new state and local taxes on personal property and any tax that applies retroactively.
SPUR's Recommendation
Prop. 42 was primarily placed on the ballot to defeat Prop. 40, a competing tax measure on billionaires. If passed, it would constrain local and state governments’ current and future ability to raise revenues for much-needed housing, transportation, infrastructure, and social services, which are already facing cuts at the federal and state levels.
Vote NO
What Prop. 42 Would Do
Proposition 42 would block state and local governments from implementing any new taxes on personal property, including retirement holdings, personal savings, real estate, stocks, and other assets. It would prohibit retroactive taxes based on a person’s prior residency status.
The measure is designed to nullify Prop. 40 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-40-billionaire-tax), which imposes a one-time excise tax of 5% on billionaires based on retroactive residency.
The Backstory
Federal bill H.R. 1, known as the “Big Beautiful Bill,” was enacted in July 2025 and will make heavy cuts to critical social safety net programs across the state, including about $19 billion in annual cuts to Medi-Cal, which covers half of children aged 0 to 5 and nearly 15 million low-income Californians. 1 Funding cuts are projected to accelerate hospital closures across California, particularly in rural areas. They are also expected to heavily impact food assistance programs such as CalFresh and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), which serves an estimated 5 million Californians.
The proposed Prop. 40 billionaire tax aims to help offset federal funding cuts. It would create a new tax on wealth, including financial assets such as stocks and intellectual property that California does not currently tax, and would apply retroactively to billionaires residing in California on or after January 1, 2026. California currently taxes income and property such as real estate, but not financial assets or other forms of wealth.
Prop. 42 was placed on the ballot through a signature-gathering effort led by Building a Better California, which is funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other billionaires, to counter Prop. 40. It requires a simple majority to pass (50% plus one vote). If both Prop. 42 and Prop. 40 pass, the measure receiving more votes would prevail. (Building a Better California has also placed Prop. 41 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-41-audits-special-taxes), a separate countermeasure to Prop. 40, on the ballot.)
Equity Impacts
California’s current tax system disproportionately benefits high-income households, while lower-income households bear a greater burden from high housing costs and regressive taxes such as property and sales taxes. 2 California’s practice of not taxing inherited wealth and financial assets contributes to income inequality and persistent racial disparities. U.S. Census data show that low-income families in California are much more likely to be Latino or Black, while most high-income families are white or Asian.
This proposition, which restricts new taxes on personal property, including retirement holdings, personal savings, real estate, stocks, and other assets, would block efforts to create new progressive tax policies to fund important priorities, including health care, food assistance, and other programs that disproportionately benefit lower-income Californians and communities of color.
Pro
Banning retroactive taxes would create more predictability for taxpayers.
Cons
Prop. 42 was placed on the ballot to block a competing measure. It could affect the state’s ability to raise revenue from other tax measures in the future.

content.text:
**No.** This is my judgment on a disputed political question, and a "yes" vote is a reasonable choice if you want California to never have a wealth tax.

Prop 42 would amend the state constitution in two ways:

- **New tax ban:** the state could never create a new tax on owning personal property. That covers stocks, business stakes, savings, retirement accounts and belongings, but not real estate.
- **Backdated tax ban:** most new taxes could not reach back to earlier income, actions or residency. The only exception is a law passed by the Legislature during a governor-declared emergency, reaching back at most one year, with the money spent on that emergency.

Its main purpose is to cancel Prop 40, the one-time 5% billionaire tax. If both pass and 42 gets more yes votes, 40 is void.

**Reasons for no:**
- **It doesn't protect your 401(k) from any real proposal.** There is no plan to tax middle-class retirement accounts. Prop 40 itself excludes them, and every past wealth-tax bill targeted the very rich and died in the Legislature.
- **You don't need it to stop Prop 40.** If you oppose the billionaire tax, you can just vote no on 40. Recent polls show 40 losing (UC Berkeley's IGS: 42% yes, 50% no; PPIC: 46% yes, 52% no).
- **The side effects are broad and permanent.** Undoing it would take another statewide vote. The backdating ban is stricter than current federal law. It could block a common budget move: tax changes passed in June that apply to the whole year, as in 2020 and 2024. It could also hamper rules meant to stop people dodging a tax they know is coming.
- **Its scope may end up in court.** Prop 40's own authors argue it could affect future vehicle license fee changes and even Prop 3. The campaign rejects this, and these critics aren't neutral.
- **Groups that didn't back the billionaire tax still oppose 42.** The SF Chronicle, League of Women Voters and SPUR took no position on 40 but oppose 42. The Mercury News/East Bay Times opposed both, saying it could have supported 42 if it had only cancelled 40.

**Reasons for yes:**
- **Endorsements:** Gov. Newsom, the state Chamber of Commerce, the California Taxpayers Association, the Republican Party, firefighter and police unions, and the San Diego Union-Tribune and Orange County Register.
- **Economic case:** Hoover Institution analysts say a firm promise of no wealth tax could keep wealthy residents, who pay a large share of state income tax, from leaving.
- **Fairness:** taxing people for income or residency from before a tax was passed is unfair.

**No**
